title: 1-bit and 2-bit Characters Problem

notes: The final bit is always 0, so the last character is either a one-bit character or the second bit of a two-bit character.
Scan from left to right, consuming one bit for 0 and two bits for 1, then check whether the scan lands on the final bit.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Read 1 and 0 as the two-bit character 10, then the final 0 is a one-bit character.
Read 11 as one two-bit character and the next 10 as another two-bit character, so the final 0 is part of 10.

content.problemStatement:
We have two special characters:

* The first character can be represented by one bit `0`.
* The second character can be represented by two bits (`10` or `11`).

With a binary array `bits` that ends with `0`, output `true` if the last character must be a one-bit character.

**Example 1:**

```
Input: bits = [1,0,0]
Output: true
Explanation: The only way to decode it is two-bit character and one-bit character.
So the last character is one-bit character.
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input: bits = [1,1,1,0]
Output: false
Explanation: The only way to decode it is two-bit character and two-bit character.
So the last character is not one-bit character.
```

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= bits.length <= 1000`
* `bits[i]` is either `0` or `1`.

notes: The intended solution scans the bit array once and uses constant auxiliary space.
The encoding is uniquely parsed from left to right because a 1 always starts a two-bit character and a 0 always forms a one-bit character.
The final bit is guaranteed to be 0, so landing exactly on its index means it is a one-bit character.
solution.approach: Scan from the beginning and decode each character greedily: a 0 is a one-bit character, while a 1 starts a two-bit character and consumes the next bit. Stop before the final bit and return whether the scan reaches that final 0 exactly.

better.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
better.description: Use a direct left-to-right scan. At each index, consume one position for a 0 and two positions for a 1. No recursion or extra state is needed.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: The direct scan is optimal: every bit before the final position is examined at most once, and each bit determines whether the next character uses one or two positions. Return true exactly when the scan lands on the final 0.

bruteForce.complexity: O(2^n) time in the worst case and O(n) recursion space.
bruteForce.description: Try to decode the prefix recursively as either a one-bit 0 or a two-bit character 10/11 and check whether the final bit is left as a separate character. This mirrors the definition but creates unnecessary branching.

followUps: Why is a left-to-right greedy scan sufficient for this encoding?
How does the parity of the consecutive 1s immediately before the final 0 determine the answer?
What would change if the array were not guaranteed to end with 0?
